A **monitor** is an output device. It needs power and a picture signal from the computer.

## Analog and digital in three steps

::: {.tej-image-hero}
![A grey continuous analog waveform with red digital samples over it.](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/file/Digital.signal.discret.svg)
:::

::: {.tej-signal-steps}
<div><strong>1</strong>Analog waveform changes continuously</div>
<div><strong>2</strong>Measure it at set intervals</div>
<div><strong>3</strong>Represent samples as digital values</div>
:::

*Figure 1. Grey is the continuous source signal. Red points are discrete, quantized digital samples. Public-domain image by Rbj and wdwd. [Open image source.](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Digital.signal.discret.svg)*

**VGA is analog.** Noise can appear as blur, colour shifts, or ghosting.

**HDMI, DisplayPort, Mini DisplayPort, USB-C video, and DVI-D are digital.** A weak digital link may show sparkles, dropouts, or no picture. DVI-A is analog. DVI-I can carry both.

## Match the port to the cable

Each pair shows a **cable plug** and the matching **computer or display port**.

Analog video. Usually no audio. Tighten the two thumb screws gently.

### DVI

DVI-D is digital. DVI-A is analog. DVI-I supports both. Check the pin pattern before connecting.

<p class="tej-caption"><a href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Dvi-cable.jpg">Cable source</a> · <a href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Computer_DVI_connector.jpg">port source</a></p>

Digital video and audio. The full-size connector has one clipped corner.

<p class="tej-caption"><a href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DisplayPort-rid.jpg">Cable source</a> · <a href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DisplayPort_on_a_computer.jpg">port source</a></p>

### Mini DisplayPort

The same DisplayPort signal in a smaller connector. Thunderbolt 1 and 2 use the same shape, so check the symbol.

<p class="tej-caption"><a href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mini_displayport.jpg">Cable source</a> · <a href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mini_DisplayPort_on_Apple_MacBook.jpg">port source</a></p>

### FireWire / IEEE 1394

A legacy digital peripheral connection for cameras, audio interfaces, and external drives. It is not a normal monitor connection.

<p class="tej-caption"><a href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FireWire_cables.jpg">Cable source</a> · <a href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FireWire-PCI-Card.jpg">port source</a></p>
:::
:::

![USB-C cable plug.](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/file/USB_Type-C.jpg)
![USB-C port and its matching cable plug.](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/file/OnePlus_3_USB_port_and_the_cable.jpg)

::: {.tej-port-copy}
### USB-C video

The shape alone does not promise video. The computer port, cable, adapter or dock, and monitor must support the same video path.

<p class="tej-caption"><a href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:USB_Type-C.jpg">Cable source</a> · <a href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:OnePlus_3_USB_port_and_the_cable.jpg">port source</a></p>
:::
:::
::::

## Connect the monitor

1. Connect monitor power and turn it on.
2. Connect a supported cable from the computer output to the matching monitor input.
3. Select that input on the monitor.
4. No picture? Check power, input choice, cable seating, adapter direction, and video support.
